paper_title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce LongBanana, to our knowledge the first expert-designed and expert-verified benchmark for long-context multi-reference image synthesis in the age of agent-driven image generation. The task requires retrieving dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, binding entities and relations, and composing one coherent final image from multiple references. LongBanana contains 90 carefully designed tasks organized by a 3-by-3 taxonomy; each task includes about 32 reference images, 20 constraints, and 50 evaluation items, yielding 4,670 expert-specified atomic evaluation items in total. Its graph-grounded evaluation design instantiates each task with reference images and an entity-relation graph, then converts node, edge, and whole-graph obligations into checklist items for Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Reviewed expert labels include a 15% double-labeled subset with 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. We further introduce LongBanana-Gen, an agent-harness framework for long-horizon image generation; experiments show that minimal agent harnesses improve over direct generation, while a ReAct-Plan-Exec-Reflect (RPR) workflow yields harness-dependent gains by strengthening evidence grounding and repair. Together, LongBanana provides an auditable testbed for measuring dense visual evidence use and a shared target for developing stronger agent-driven image-generation systems. Code and data are available at the project page: https://long-banana.com/.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A useful image-generation system [4, 6, 16, 36] should be able to synthesize new image from the visual evidence provided by the user, even when that evidence is spread across many references. Consider an accessories retailer preparing an advertisement for all handbags with dual parallel top handles (Figure 1). The system must inspect large inventory, select the relevant bags, reject visually similar distractors, preserve appearance details, and arrange the selected items according to the requested composition. The output may look realistic while still being wrong: it may use the wrong handbag, bind handle style to the wrong object, violate count or layout constraint, or introduce unsupported details. The central capability is therefore not visual plausibility alone, but reference-grounded synthesis across retrieval, rejection, binding, and composition. *Equal contribution. Work done during internship in KlingAI Research. Project lead. Corresponding authors. 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Track on Evaluations and Datasets. Figure 1: LONGBANANA task overview. (a) Each case pairs heterogeneous reference set and structured synthesis prompt with the generated image under evaluation. (b) LONGBANANA-Eval converts graph-grounded checklist items into dimension-level scores and auditable evidence traces. The score labels Content, Relations, and Global denote Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction, respectively. Evaluating this capability raises central question: how can we tell whether an image-generation system has synthesized correct image from long, multi-reference visual context? The difficulty is not only that such tasks contain more images or longer prompts. The required evidence is distributed across references, entities, attributes, relations, hard negatives, unsupported-content rules, and intermediate decisions. Success can only be judged by checking whether the final image satisfies the reference-grounded obligations. benchmark therefore needs dense multi-reference tasks and scoring that localizes errors rather than holistic score. Current image-generation benchmarks [14, 29] capture important parts of this problem, but leave the full measurement target under-specified. Research on instruction-guided editing, personalization, and prompt following addresses local edits and textual requirements [2, 10, 14, 45, 51, 56]. Recent multi-reference benchmarks move closer to reference-based synthesis [3, 23, 37], and automatic evaluation methods support systematic assessment [39, 47, 53]. What remains difficult to measure is dense evidence use: whether the model selected the right references, rejected plausible distractors, attached attributes and relations to the correct entities, and avoided content that is unsupported by either the instruction or the references. realistic image can pass surface-level inspection while failing exactly these obligations. These failures are typically provenance errors rather than rendering errors, where provenance is the sourcea specific reference, or the instruction itselfto which each piece of generated content should be attributed: system may render the right object category while copying appearance from the wrong reference, place the correct entities while violating their relation, or produce polished composition that leaks hard negative into the scene. To make such errors measurable, we model each task as an entityrelation graph. Its nodes are the entities, attributes, and text elements that must (or must not) appear; its edges are the spatial, interaction, ordering, and local-appearance relations that bind those entities; and its whole-graph constraints are scene-level obligationslayout, counts, temporal state, and reference selectionthat no single node or edge captures. We refer to node, an edge, or whole-graph constraint as graph unit. These three levels define the three graph-grounded scoring dimensions used throughout the paper: Content Fidelity (node level), Relational Binding (edge level), and Global Constraint Satisfaction (whole-graph level). We derive checklist of atomic, visually verifiable items, each tied to one graph unit, to localize failures. 2 To make this benchmark auditable at scale, we design LONGBANANA-Eval, graph-grounded checklist evaluation pipeline whose scorer LONGBANANAEVAL acts as an agentic checklist judge (Section 3): rather than judging the final image with one undifferentiated score, it routes each checklist item to rubric-guided critic, invokes deterministic toolsOCR, counting, layout, and identity checkswhen an item benefits from an executable check, and records evidence traces for quality control and reproducibility. We validate this measurement target on human-audited pool of 900 generated outputs with 46,700 reviewed checklist labels. An independently double-labeled subset of 7,005 labels (15%) reaches 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted κ, and these reviewed expert checklist scores serve as the reference standard against which we validate LONGBANANAEVAL. We also use LONGBANANA to study agent-driven image-generation workflows. Each system wraps fixed image generator in an agent harness [30, 40, 54]: the harness maintains reference state, selects evidence, schedules prompts, invokes the generator, and revises requests, while the image generator only synthesizes pixels. We evaluate direct generation, minimal agent harnesses, and RPRenabled harnesses, where RPR is serial workflow combining ReAct evidence grounding, PlanExec decomposition, and Reflect-based revision (Section 4), and we compare multiple image generators under fixed harness. Across these settings, agent harnesses improve the aggregate profile over direct generation, yet no single harness dominates: the best per-subclass scores remain distributed across direct prompting, minimal harnesses, and RPR. RPR itself yields harness-dependent gains, helping only when the harness reliably exploits retrieved evidence and revision feedback, and otherwise introducing drift. Contributions Benchmark setting and dataset. We introduce LONGBANANA-Bench for long-context multi-reference image synthesis, with 90 expert-designed cases, dense references, hard negatives, unsupported-content rules, and 3 3 taxonomy. Graph-grounded evaluation. We introduce LONGBANANA-Eval, mapping entityrelation graphs to atomic checklist items over Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction. Expert verification and audit protocol. We provide reviewed expert checklist labels, agreement statistics, evidence traces, and scorer validation against human labels. Agent-driven generation study. We evaluate direct, harness-based, and RPR workflows to show that current systems fail in structured, diagnosable ways rather than along single image-quality axis.

sections.title: 2 The LONGBANANA Benchmark
sections.content: 2.1 Goal and Scope LONGBANANA is an evaluation benchmark for long-horizon multi-reference image synthesis. system is given heterogeneous reference set and structured synthesis instruction, and must render one coherent image that satisfies the obligations of the tasks entityrelation graph (Section 1): its required and forbidden nodes, the edges that bind them, and the whole-graph constraints on the scene. The setting differs from low-reference editing because the decisive evidence is distributed across many images, and correctness is measured by the graph-derived checklist of atomic, visually verifiable items rather than by single holistic quality score. LONGBANANA contains 90 cases: 10 cases for each subclass in 3 3 taxonomy. typical case contains approximately 32 references and more than 20 cross-reference constraints, and across the benchmark experts specify 4,670 atomic checklist items. Because every item is tied to single graph unit, each failure is localized to specific obligation rather than absorbed into an overall score. 2.2 Task Taxonomy and Evaluation Rubric We organize LONGBANANA tasks into three-suite taxonomy that captures their primary synthesis demands (Figure 2). Across these tasks, shared graph-grounded rubric evaluates whether the generated image preserves the required content, relations, and scene-level constraints. 3 Figure 2: The 3 3 taxonomy used to organize LONGBANANA. Rows group cases into Scene Composition, Visual Appearance, and Reference Reasoning, while columns expose subclass-level demands used for diagnostic reporting. Each subclass contributes 10 cases. The three suites are Scene Composition (semantic coverage, relational graph consistency, and layout arrangement), Visual Appearance (global appearance conditioning, local appearance binding, and appearance harmonization), and Reference Reasoning (selection and retrieval, temporal/state reasoning, and counting/aggregation). All tasks require final image output; subclasses differ in the evidence-integration behavior being tested. For each case, checklist items assess correctness at three levels of the entityrelation graph: nodes, edges, and the whole graph. Content Fidelity measures node-level correctness: required entities, attributes, text elements, and supported semantic nodes must appear, while forbidden or unsupported nodes must be absent. Relational Binding measures edge-level correctness, including spatial relations, interactions, ordering, support, containment, and local bindings such as texture, material, color, pose, or state assigned to specific entity. Global Constraint Satisfaction measures whole-graph correctness, including composition, layout, scene-level style, count and aggregation constraints, temporal/state constraints, and reference-selection constraints. This graph-grounded rubric localizes failures to specific content, bindings, or scene-level obligations, supporting consistent diagnosis across task categories and generation systems. 2.3 Benchmark Construction We construct each case around shared entityrelation graph that connects the synthesis instruction, reference images, and evaluation checklist (Figure 3). Construction proceeds from scenario description to structured constraints, then to the visual references and instruction that express the task, and finally to the checklist used to evaluate its result. Scenario and graph construction. Expert authors design scenarios aligned with the task taxonomy, drawing on storyboard, product, and scene-composition use cases. scenario specifies what the final image should depict and which entities, visual attributes, and interactions must be preserved. An LLM then structures the scenario into an entityrelation graph: nodes represent entities and their attributes, edges encode spatial relations, interactions, and local appearance bindings, and whole-graph constraints specify requirements such as composition and counts. This representation makes the dependencies explicit. For example, an appearance requirement identifies both the visual property and the entity to which it belongs, while relational requirement identifies the entities that must participate in the requested configuration. These constraints guide both task synthesis and checklist derivation. Instruction and reference construction. The graph guides the creation of the target instruction and reference images, including entity, appearance, and optional background references. The instruction expresses the requested composition and the relationships to be realized; the references supply the visual identities, local details, and appearance cues needed to instantiate it. Discriminative visual attributes are retained in the references and omitted from text where possible. Because these cues are distributed across images, the generator must associate each relevant reference with the intended 4 Figure 3: LONGBANANA construction pipeline. (1) Scenario Construction: experts design scenarios aligned with the task taxonomy. (2) Graph Construction: an LLM structures each scenario into entities, attributes, relations, and whole-scene constraints. (3) Prompt & Reference Synthesis: the graph guides the creation of the target instruction and visual references. (4) Checklist & Curation: graph constraints are translated into evidence-linked checklist items, and human curators review the instruction, references, and checklist for consistency, visual feasibility, and verifiability. graph entity and combine their evidence while maintaining the requested relations. At least 30 cases also include two or more hard-negative references that are visually plausible but irrelevant to the requested output. Their exclusion is encoded in the checklist, allowing distractor leakage to be assessed alongside the inclusion of required content. Checklist derivation. We translate graph constraints into atomic checklist items using the rubric introduced in Section 2.2. Node-level items check required entities and attributes; edge-level items check relations and appearance bindings; whole-graph items check scene-wide requirements such as layout and counts. Each item records an observable condition, the graph unit it evaluates, the relevant reference images, and its scoring criteria. This links judgment about the output to the evidence needed to make it. Positive items test whether required condition is satisfied, while negative items check for the absence of distractor or unsupported content. Each completed case therefore pairs an instruction and reference set with checklist derived from the same task constraints. Section 3 describes how these items are scored. Case curation. Human curators review the instruction, reference images, and checklist together, checking their correspondence to the task graph. They inspect whether the references visibly support the required identities and attributes, whether the requested relations and composition are visually feasible, and whether checklist items express clear, individually verifiable conditions. They also check reference density, constraint coverage, and overlapping or ambiguous items. Requirements that cannot be judged from the references and candidate output are revised or rejected before inclusion. Appendix provides the detailed construction protocol and case specifications. Section 4 describes human labeling of generated outputs to establish reference judgments for evaluator validation.

sections.title: 3 LONGBANANA-Eval: Graph-Grounded Checklist Evaluation
sections.content: LONGBANANA-Eval evaluates generated image against the cases graph-derived checklist. Its agentic checklist judge, LONGBANANAEVAL, prepares item-specific reference evidence, routes each check to dimension-specific critic, and combines the resulting judgments into dimension-level and overall scores. As shown in Figure 4, the pipeline also records the evidence supporting each item judgment. 5 3.1 Checklist Scoring Protocol Evidence preparation and routing. For each item, the parser reads the condition to verify, its rubric dimension, reference identifiers, and scoring criteria from the case specification. It assembles the generated image and relevant reference images into an evidence packet, with optional crops to localize the region under inspection. Negative-content checks additionally receive the identifiers and roles of applicable hard-negative references. The router assigns the packet to the critic corresponding to the items rubric dimension. Dimension-specific checks and tools. The Content Fidelity critic checks required entities, attributes, and text, together with the absence of forbidden or distractor content. The Relational Binding critic checks spatial and interaction relations and the assignment of local appearance cues to their intended entities. The Global Constraint Satisfaction critic checks scene-wide requirements, including layout, global style, counts, and temporal or state constraints. Each critic compares the output with the items reference evidence and may invoke verification tools: OCR for readable text, detection or counting for multiplicity, layout routines for spatial constraints, and identity or feature matching for consistency. The critic combines these observations with the visual evidence to determine whether the item is satisfied. Item judgments and evidence traces. Each check produces label sj {0, 1, 2}: 2 for satisfied requirement, 1 for partial satisfaction or uncertain evidence, and 0 for an unsatisfied requirement. For negative items, the requirement is the absence of forbidden or unsupported content: complete absence scores 2, ambiguous or suspicious leakage scores 1, and clear erroneous appearance scores 0. The evidence trace associates the label with the relevant references, the critics findings, and any tool observations. Traces are organized by the same three rubric dimensions, linking each reported judgment to the evidence used to reach it. Score aggregation. For generated image with checklist items, the overall score is the mean item label scaled to 010. Dimension scores apply the same calculation to the item set Jd assigned to dimension d: Soverall = 5 (cid:88) j=1 sj, Sd = 5 Jd (cid:88) jJd sj. The dimension scores provide diagnostic profile, while the overall score summarizes the full checklist. The main generation tables express checklist-average scores on 0100 scale; Section 4 separately defines the difficulty-weighted task pass rate, P@70%. Baseline and validation. The VLM-as-judge baseline receives the generated image, relevant references, and checklist in single judging call and returns item labels for the same score aggregation. It shares the judging backbone and item-level criteria with LONGBANANAEVAL, whose execution organizes evidence and tool use around individual checks. Section 4 evaluates both judges against reviewed human labels at the item and output-score levels; implementation details appear in Appendix C.

sections.content: Our experiments connect evaluator validation with study of long-context image generation. We first establish agreement between automatic checklist judgments and reviewed human labels. We then ask how much explicit graph structure helps non-agentic generator, what adaptive agentic workflows add beyond an optimized static plan, and how those gains interact with the image backend. 4.1 Protocol and Metrics Generation conditions. The broad Nano Banana 2 advantage shows that backend capability remains consequential even under the strongest evaluated workflow. Diagnostic implications. The comparison with PD-Direct highlights the distinction between planning composition and controlling its realization. PD-Direct uses privileged graph information to optimize reference grouping and ordering, then executes that schedule in stages. The resulting images can still depart from the intended constraints as entities are added or edited. Agentic workflows can inspect intermediate outputs, revisit reference evidence, and adjust subsequent actions. Their broader advantage motivates treating the evolving visual state, alongside the task structure, as central to generation control. The checklist turns this control problem into inspectable requirements. PD-Directs strong appearance conditioning alongside its weaker reference selection and state reasoning directs attention to evidence use across composition steps. Item judgments and evidence traces can distinguish an incorrect reference choice from an incorrect entity binding or an unmet scene-wide requirement. For future agent designs, these diagnostics offer basis for choosing what to revisit and what to preserve during revision. The resulting research target is evidence-guided adaptation: connect inspection of the current image to the next retrieval, generation, or repair action while preserving satisfied constraints. Further analyses. Appendix reports the workflow ablation and case-paired score diagnostics. The generation comparisons, component study, and item-level traces together connect aggregate performance to the decisions made during synthesis, providing basis for developing more capable reference-grounded image-generation agents.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: LONGBANANA establishes long-context multi-reference image synthesis as benchmark for integrating dispersed visual evidence, rejecting distractors, and satisfying coupled content and relational constraints. LONGBANANA-Bench provides 90 expert-designed and expert-verified cases across 3 3 taxonomy, with 4,670 atomic checklist items. LONGBANANA-Eval turns these constraints into evidence-linked judgments, validated against human labels, to measure constraint fulfillment and localize generation failures. The generation study highlights the distinction between optimizing composition plan and adaptively controlling its realization. PD-Direct combines privileged access to the construction graph with exactly optimized staging, establishing competitive non-agentic baseline. Agentic workflows achieve broader success without direct access to that graph, showing the value of adaptive evidence use and generation control beyond fixed schedule. The RPR component study further supports coordinating retrieval, execution, and repair within one workflow. These findings point toward agents that reason over both task structure and the evolving visual state, preserve reference bindings across steps, and target unmet requirements during revision.

sections.title: A Related Work
sections.content: Image Synthesis Benchmarks. Image-generation benchmarks cover instruction-guided editing, personalization, human alignment, and reasoning-oriented synthesis [22, 24, 28, 29, 46, 48] but generally focus on creating single image from single prompt. Recent multi-reference benchmarks [3, 23, 37, 42] are closer to our setting, but they typically use fewer references or lower-density cross-image constraints. LONGBANANA targets final-image synthesis in which correctness depends on retrieving, rejecting, binding, and integrating evidence distributed across dozens of references. Atomic Constraint Evaluation. Long-context tasks have long been central challenge across language and vision domains [1, 18, 19, 23, 41]. Instruction-following benchmarks in NLP often convert open-ended tasks into verifiable atomic requirements. IFEval [55] emphasizes directly checkable constraints, and TIFA [11] converts text-to-image faithfulness into question-answer checks. LONGBANANA transfers this principle to long-horizon multi-reference synthesis. Each checklist item links the output to graph node, graph edge, or whole-graph constraint, so failures can be traced to missing content, incorrect relations, hard-negative leakage, unsupported content, or global constraint violations. Automatic Judges. Low-level metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [12, 35, 49] are poorly matched to reference faithfulness, motivating model-based judges and rubric evaluators [5, 79, 15, 20, 26, 27, 33, 38, 43, 44, 52, 53, 57, 58]. However, holistic judge can conflate realism with correctness when many references are present [17, 21, 32, 34, 50]. LONGBANANAEVAL evaluates checklist-level evidence with routed critics and tools, and we report its validity through Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall agreement with reviewed expert labels [13, 25, 31].

B.7 Checklist Item Template checklist item is valid only if it is visually verifiable, reference-grounded, and non-redundant where possible. Positive items evaluate whether required fact is present and correctly bound. Negative items are Content Fidelity checks that evaluate whether distractor or unsupported element is absent: completely absent is labeled 2, visually suspicious or ambiguous leakage is labeled 1, and full erroneous appearance is labeled 0. Items requiring specialist interpretation include short reference note identifying the evidence to inspect. B.8 Annotation Interface and Protocol Annotators view the reference set, target instruction, generated output, checklist item evidence, and explicit 0/1/2 scoring instructions. The human-audited multi-system output pool covers all 90 cases and all 10 reported generation conditions, yielding 900 generated outputs. Human reviewers assign 46,700 reviewed checklist labels by applying all 4,670 benchmark checklist items to every reported condition. The three rubric dimensions are computed from the corresponding checklist labels. The protocol uses primary annotation, second-pass review, third-pass expert adjudication, an independently double-labeled subset of 7,005 labels, stratified audit sampling, schema validation, and score-stability checks. The annotation audit records include qualification and training criteria, review status, correction logs, adjudication logs, audit outcomes, and stability summaries without exposing annotator identities. Figures 5 and 6 show screenshots from the checklist annotation platform used for these human reviews. B.9 Expert Label Quality Control Table 8 summarizes label quality control. All 46,700 judgments undergo review and adjudication, with difficult items receiving further review to establish final labels. Errors found in the random audit trigger expanded checks of related labels, and the label set is frozen after all revisions. The radar profiles are intended as compact diagnostics of subclass-level failure patterns, not as additional statistical tests. Figure 17: Radar profiles for the two primary result comparisons. Left: strategy comparison with Nano Banana 2 fixed as the image generator. Right: image-generator comparison with OpenClaw + RPR fixed as the harness. Axes are LONGBANANA taxonomy subclasses; values are the checklistaverage subclass scores (0100) reported in the main tables. D.1 Direct Baseline Implementations FP-Direct uses the full target prompt throughout generation and varies only the visible reference window. Because case may contain more reference images than the backend can consume at once, the implementation uses window of eight references and iterates over the ordered reference inventory, e.g., ref1ref8, ref9ref16, and so on until all non-background references have been exposed. Each round receives the same complete target prompt; there is no entity-level batching, graph-conditioned relation filtering, explicit state memory, or repair step. PD-Direct is deterministic staged-composition baseline rather than free-form planning agent. It uses the same eight-reference backend budget as FP-Direct, but allocates that budget by graph structure rather than by inventory order. Each non-background entity node is represented by one reference image. Starting from the pre-generated background image, PD-Direct composes nonbackground entities in ordered batches of at most eight entity references, following the staging schedule that is optimal for the cases entityrelation graph. Let b(v) {1, . . . , K} be the batch index of entity v, with = N/8, at most eight entity references per batch, and the background fixed at batch 0. Over the (unweighted, directed, possibly cyclic) entityrelation graph = (V, E), the schedule minimizes lexicographic objective: first the number of relations (u, v) whose anchor is composed later than its dependent, {(u, v) : b(u) > b(v)}, capacity-constrained feedbackarc count that we minimize exactly by integer programming, and, among schedules attaining that minimum, the total relational stretch (cid:80) (u,v)Eb(u) b(v). We solve it exactly with an integer program (Pass 1 minimizes the feedback count ; Pass 2 minimizes the stretch subject to the feedback count equal to ); each case has small number of composed entities (N 32), so the integer program solves in seconds. At step zero the backend receives the background image plus the first batchs reference images and produces intermediate_00.png; at each later step it receives the previous intermediate image plus the next batchs references, and the final intermediate is saved as target/target_image.png. For case with = 32 composed entities this yields = N/8 = 4 batches and four intermediate images. The prompt at each step is constructed deterministically from fixed staged-composition instructions, the scene prompt, the entity types in the current batch, and all graph edges incident to that batch (there is no per-step cap on edges, so every relation is presented at the step of its later endpoint), followed by constraints to preserve existing content and maintain consistent lighting, scale, and perspective. Reference images and the background are generated upstream from the entity catalog, scene specification, and entityrelation graph; PD-Direct only stages their use during target construction. D.2 Agent-Orchestrator Component Ablation Figure 18 summarizes the ReAct, PlanExec, and Reflect stages used by the full RPR workflow. Table 11 isolates these stages with OpenClaw and Nano Banana 2 fixed, comparing the minimal OpenClaw harness, each single-stage variant, and the full OpenClaw + RPR stack. For this ablation, item difficulty is computed from the mean normalized item score across the five configurations in this table, using the thresholds in Appendix C.4. The resulting weights are shared across all five rows. Subclass scores, Overall Avg., and P@70% therefore use this within-table relative difficulty calibration rather than the main benchmarks frozen reference-pool weights. PlanExec alone gives the strongest Visual Appearance scores on GAC and LAB, consistent with decomposition helping product, style, and material organization, but it weakens relation control and structured reasoning when evidence retrieval and repair are not coupled to the plan. ReAct alone improves selection relative to the minimal OpenClaw harness, but its overall score drops because evidence selection without explicit execution control does not reliably preserve spatial and appearance bindings through generation. Reflect alone raises LAC, AGG, and P@70%, indicating that revision helps repair visible layout and aggregation errors, but it can also over-correct or drift when missing evidence is not re-grounded. 36 The full RPR stack gives the best overall score and pass rate because the stages close each others failure modes: ReAct grounds the reference set, PlanExec turns the grounded state into an executable synthesis schedule, and Reflect supports revision based on the generated result. The remaining TSR drop relative to minimal OpenClaw suggests that temporal and state-reasoning cases are sensitive to over-revision: once physically plausible final state is found, additional repair can shift pose or event timing away from the intended state. Thus, RPR is best interpreted as an evidence-preserving orchestration pattern, not as uniformly beneficial amount of extra reasoning. sections.title: E Responsible Release and Safeguards
sections.content: E.1 Limitations The 33 taxonomy covers meaningful subset of long-horizon multi-reference synthesis, but does not cover video generation, 3D scene composition, or unrestricted multimodal planning. The benchmark is intentionally high-density, which improves diagnostic resolution but makes expert annotation expensive. LONGBANANAEVAL depends on backbone multimodal models and verification tools, so model identifiers and tool versions must accompany final results. E.2 Broader Impact Details The benchmark is designed for measurement rather than deployment, but it evaluates systems capable of generating realistic composite images from many references. Positive uses include model auditing and failure diagnosis. Risks include deceptive media, impersonation, privacy leakage, biased reference coverage, and copyright-sensitive reuse. Mitigations include filtering unsafe content, documenting provenance, restricting problematic assets, and providing project issue tracker for reporting release problems at https://github.com/TIGER-AI-Lab/LongBanana/issues.

sections.title: NeurIPS Paper Checklist
sections.content: 1. Claims Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the papers contributions and scope? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The abstract and Section 1 state the benchmark, evaluator, and empirical claims, while Sections 2 to 5 define the scope and required evidence. Run-specific factual details are provided in the anonymized OpenReview artifacts and associated run records. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper. The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers. The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings. It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper. 2. Limitations Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix discusses benchmark scope, annotation expense, and evaluator dependence. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper. The authors are encouraged to create separate Limitations section in their paper. The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be. The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on few datasets or with few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated. The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon. The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size. If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness. While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that arent acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations. 3. Theory assumptions and proofs Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and complete (and correct) proof? Answer: [N/A] Justification: The paper does not present theoretical theorems or formal proof claims. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results. All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and crossreferenced. All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems. The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide short proof sketch to provide intuition. Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material. Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced. 4. Experimental result reproducibility Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)? Answer: [No] Justification: The paper describes benchmark construction, scoring, model and harness identifiers, and baseline implementations in Sections 2 to D, but does not include executable reproduction commands or environment files. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. If the paper includes experiments, [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not. If the contribution is dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable. Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to hosted model (e.g., in the case of large language model), releasing of model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed. While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example (a) If the contribution is primarily new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm. (b) If the contribution is primarily new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully. (c) If the contribution is new model (e.g., large language model), then there should either be way to access this model for reproducing the results or way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset). (d) We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results. 5. Open access to data and code 40 Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material? Answer: [No] Justification: This preprint does not provide public data/code access link with executable reproduction instructions. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code. Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/ public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for new open-source benchmark). The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https: //neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details. The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc. The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why. At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable). Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted. 6. Experimental setting/details Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The experimental design, 90-case benchmark, evaluator configuration, metrics, and ablations are described in Sections 2 to 4. Appendix identifies the agent and judging models and the harness versions. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them. The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material. 7. Experiment statistical significance Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Section 4 reports checklist-average generation scores and the secondary difficulty-weighted P@70% diagnostic. Appendix reports case-level bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests for the checklist-average scores; judgehuman agreement is reported as correlation diagnostics. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper. 41 The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions). The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to library function, bootstrap, etc.) The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors). It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean. It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report 2-sigma error bar than state that they have 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified. For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates). If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text. 8. Experiments compute resources Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments? Answer: [No] Justification: The paper identifies the generation and judging models but does not report per-run compute resources, runtime, or API costs. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments. The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage. The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute. The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didnt make it into the paper). 9. Code of ethics Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Asset provenance and privacy screening are discussed in Appendix B; broader impacts and responsible-release safeguards are discussed in Appendix E. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics. If the authors answer [No], they should explain the special circumstances that require deviation from the Code of Ethics. The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction). 10. Broader impacts Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix discusses positive impacts for evaluation rigor and negative risks related to deceptive media, privacy, copyright, and biased coverage, together with mitigation measures. 42 Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed. If the authors answer [N/A] or [No], they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact. Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations. The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster. The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology. If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML). 11. Safeguards Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Appendix describes asset screening and redistribution restrictions; Appendix describes responsible-release safeguards and takedown/contact procedures. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks. Released models that have high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters. Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images. We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make best faith effort. 12. Licenses for existing assets Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected? Answer: [Yes] Justification: Asset provenance and licensing are documented in Sections 2 and B, covering source images, models, tools, and external benchmarks. Source citations, license/TOS audit results, and redistribution decisions are included in the submitted artifact metadata. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets. The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset. The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include URL. The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset. For scraped data from particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided. If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of dataset. For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided. If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the assets creators. 13. New assets Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The benchmark, manifests, annotation schema, scorer configuration, and documentation are described in Sections 2 to C. The dataset card, manifest, release license, and anonymized artifact access information are provided in the submitted OpenReview artifacts. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets. Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc. The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used. At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file. 14. Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)? Answer: [Yes] Justification: The annotation workflow, adjudication plan, compensation reporting, and instruction/screenshot requirements are described in Sections 2 and B. Instructions, UI screenshots, rater counts, qualification criteria, compensation rate, and annotation time are reported as annotation metadata. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects. Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper. According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector. 15. Guidelines: The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.
